statement: Ella puts 12 square tiles, each with sides of 1 cm, together to make one rectangle. What is the largest possible distance all the way round her rectangle?

choices.misconception: I added the length 12 and the width 1, but only once each.
I used the 3 by 4 rectangle, which gives the smallest distance round.
I stopped at the 2 by 6 rectangle and did not try one long row.
I counted the top and the bottom of one long row but forgot the two short ends.

hints: List every rectangle: rows times tiles in a row must make 12. Work out the distance round each one and compare. Long, thin shapes have more edge on the outside.
The rectangles are 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4. For 1 by 12, go round: 12 along the top, 1 down, 12 along the bottom, 1 up.

solutions.reliable: The rectangles made of 12 tiles are 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4. Their distances round are $12 + 1 + 12 + 1 = 26$ cm, $6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16$ cm and $4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14$ cm. The largest is 26 cm. The idea to keep: the same tiles can have very different distances round, and a long thin shape has the most.
solutions.elegant: Every tile edge that touches another tile is hidden. A single row hides the fewest edges, only 11 joins, so it shows the most outside: $12 \times 4 = 48$ edges, minus $2 \times 11 = 22$ hidden ones, gives 26. The idea to keep: to make the outside long, make the tiles touch as little as possible.

whyOnTest: Comparing all rectangles with the same tiles shows that area and distance round are different things.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
